Welcome toTwo-Level Free Energy

One ground state, many excited states, a warm reservoir — where does the probability settle?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: mean energy, entropy term and free energy of a trial distribution for a ground state and a w-fold excited level

Source

Concept
A system with one ground state at energy 0 and an excited level at energy ε shared by w states, in contact with a reservoir at temperature T. A trial distribution puts probability p₀ in the ground state and (1 − p₀)/w in each excited state. The main chart plots Ē/ε = 1 − p₀ (red), −TS/ε = (kBT/ε)[p₀ ln p₀ + (1 − p₀) ln((1 − p₀)/w)] (blue, with 0 ln 0 = 0) and F/ε = Ē/ε − TS/ε (heavy curve) against p₀ on fixed axes. The inset plots the Boltzmann ground-state probability p₀eq = 1/(1 + w e−ε/kBT) against kBT/ε for the selected w, with a dot at the current temperature.
Serves
Explaining where a system held at fixed temperature places its probability, and how temperature and the degeneracy w decide it. Energies are in units of ε and temperature is kBT/ε; for ε = 0.100 eV the kelvin value is shown under the temperature slider (kB = 8.617×10−5 eV/K).
Inquiry
Five questions and a closing summary, each asking the student to set the temperature and w, drag the trial p₀ or sweep the temperature, and compare the readouts in the Readouts panel below the controls.
Misconception
Common expectations about where the probability goes when kBT is below the gap are probed through the answer choices, not stated on screen.

Pedagogy principles applied

Commit, then checkEach question is a gated choice card; the student commits to an answer and checks it on the chart and readouts.
Operational quantitiesĒ/ε, −TS/ε, F/ε, p₀eq and the equilibrium free energy −kBT ln Z are read to three decimals from the same functions that draw the curves.
Stable scaleBoth charts use fixed axes (energy −3.6 to 1.2 in units of ε; p₀ from 0 to 1; kBT/ε from 0 to 0.50), so every control change is visible as a real change.
Direct manipulationThe trial p₀ is set by dragging the grey line on the chart or by the slider; the curves redraw at once.
Nothing pre-markedThe minimum of F, the equilibrium value on the main chart and the half-way crossing in the inset are left unmarked for the student to find.
Honest unitsEnergies in units of ε, temperature as kBT/ε, with its kelvin value for ε = 0.100 eV.
Formal layer on demandThe derivations live in The Physics sheet, opened from the header.
The Free Energy of a Two-Level System
✦Teach me
Mean energy, entropy term and free energy of a trial distribution
Equilibrium ground-state probability p0eq against kBT/ε, for the selected w

Guided Inquiry

1 · Finding the lowest F

Keep w = 1 and kBT/ε = 0.20. Move the trial p0 from 0 to 1, by dragging the grey line or with the slider, watching the F readout. Where is F lowest, and how does that compare with the equilibrium readout p0eq?

2 · Adding upper states

Keep kBT/ε = 0.20 and step w from 1 up to 10, 100 and 1000, watching the p0eq readout. What happens to the equilibrium ground-state probability?

3 · Energy against entropy

Keep w = 1000 and kBT/ε = 0.20. Move the trial p0 from 1.00 down to the value where F is lowest, watching Ē, −TS and F. Which statement describes what happens?

4 · Where p0 passes one half

Keep w = 1000. Starting from kBT/ε = 0.50, lower the temperature in steps of 0.01 with the − button, down to 0.05, watching the dot in the inset and the p0eq readout. At what temperature does the ground-state probability pass one half?

5 · How the crossing depends on w

Repeat the sweep with w = 10 and then with w = 100, finding where p0eq passes one half each time. How does that temperature depend on w?

6 · Energy against entropy

At a fixed temperature a system settles where F = Ē − TS is lowest, not where Ē is lowest. That minimum always sits at the Boltzmann value p0eq = 1/(1 + we−ε/kBT).

Low energy pulls the probability into the ground state; entropy pulls it into the level with more states. The two are equally likely exactly when kBT ln w = ε, so a highly degenerate level wins at temperatures well below the gap.

The Physics

The Free Energy of a Two-Level System · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A system has one ground state at energy 0 and an excited level at energy ε shared by w states, and it is held at temperature T by a reservoir. This sim plots Ē/ε, −TS/ε and F/ε for a trial distribution, against p0, the probability put in the ground state.

What you'll learn

  • How F = Ē − TS is built from a mean energy and an entropy term.
  • What a trial distribution is, and how p0 sets both terms.
  • How kBT/ε and w decide the numbers you read from the chart.
The model: one ground state, and an excited level of w states a gap ε above it.

What's on screen

  • Red line: the mean energy Ē/ε. Blue line: the entropy term −TS/ε.
  • Heavy curve: the free energy F/ε = Ē/ε − TS/ε.
  • Grey vertical line: the trial p0, with a dot on each curve. Drag it along the chart.
  • Strip below the chart: p0eq against kBT/ε for the selected w, with a dot at the current temperature.
  • Readouts: a Trial distribution card and an Equilibrium (Boltzmann) card.
See itOpen the sim at its present settings. Watch for: the three curves, the grey line at your trial p0 with a dot on each curve, and the readouts for that trial.

03

A trial distribution has a mean energy and an entropy

A trial puts probability p0 on the ground state and (1 − p0)/w on each excited state. Only the excited level carries energy, so the mean energy is Ē = (1 − p0)ε. The entropy is S = −kB ∑ p ln p over the states, and the sim plots −TS, which for this trial reads as below, with 0 ln 0 = 0.

Both terms in units of ε.

Their sum is the free energy of the trial (notes 4.56), shown as the heavy curve.

The free energy of the trial.

The two terms depend on p0 in different ways, so F does too. At the opening setting, kBT = 0.20 ε, w = 1 and p0 = 0.50, the readouts give Ē/ε = 0.500, −TS/ε = −0.139 and F/ε = +0.361. Low Ē calls for probability in the ground state and large S for probability spread out, and F puts the two on one scale.

See itKeep kBT/ε = 0.20 and w = 1, with p0 at 0.50. Watch for: the grey line at the middle of the chart with a dot on each curve, and the Trial distribution card reading 0.500, −0.139 and +0.361.
04

F is lowest at the Boltzmann value of p0

A system at fixed temperature settles where F is smallest. For this model that is p0eq = 1/Z, with Z = 1 + w e−ε/kBT the partition function, and the lowest value is F = −kBT ln Z (notes 4.57). The excited level enters Z once for each of its w states (notes 4.4).

The Boltzmann value of p0 and the lowest F.

At kBT = 0.20 ε the factor e−5 is 0.00674. With w = 1, Z = 1.0067, so p0eq = 0.993 and F = −0.0013 ε. The minimum sits next to p0 = 1, with almost all the probability in the ground state, while F climbs to +1.000 ε at p0 = 0.

w = 1 at kBT = 0.20 ε. The vertical range is shorter than the sim’s, so the shallow minimum shows.
See itKeep kBT/ε = 0.20 and w = 1, and put p0 at 0.99. Watch for: the circle marking the lowest F just left of the right-hand edge, F/ε reading −0.001, and p0eq reading 0.993 in the Equilibrium card.
05

A many-fold excited level can hold most of the probability

At kBT = 0.20 ε each excited state is e−5 = 0.00674 times as likely as the ground state, which is small. But the level has w states, so as a whole it carries the weight w e−5 against 1 for the ground state, and p0eq = 1/(1 + w e−5).

ww e−5p0eqexcited level’s share
10.00670.9930.007
100.0670.9370.063
1000.6740.5970.403
10006.740.1290.871

Stepping w from 1 to 1000 drops p0eq through 0.993, 0.937, 0.597 and 0.129. At w = 1000 the level weighs 6.74 against 1, and holds 87% of the probability, even though each of its states is less likely than the ground state.

How the equilibrium probability is shared, from the table above.
See itKeep kBT/ε = 0.20 and set w to 100, with p0 at 0.60. Watch for: p0eq reading 0.597, with the circle marking the lowest F near the grey line.
See itKeep kBT/ε = 0.20 and set w to 1000, with p0 at 0.13. Watch for: p0eq reading 0.129, and the lowest F lying well to the left of where it sat for w = 1.
06

Energy rises but the entropy term falls further

Take w = 1000 at kBT = 0.20 ε and start with all the probability in the ground state, p0 = 1, where Ē, −TS and F are all 0. Move p0 down to 0.13. Probability now sits in the level at ε, so Ē rises by 0.870 ε. Spreading it over 1000 states raises S, so −TS falls, by 1.279 ε. The fall wins: F drops to −0.409 ε, which is −kBT ln Z = −0.2 ln 7.74.

w = 1000 at kBT = 0.20 ε. The dashed line marks p0 = 0.13.

Go on to p0 = 0 and Ē reaches 1.000 ε, so F climbs back to −0.382 ε, still below its value at p0 = 1. The lowest F is a compromise, and its place is set by the ratio of the level’s weight to the ground state’s.

See itKeep kBT/ε = 0.20 and set w to 1000, with p0 at 1.00. Watch for: all three readouts at 0.000 and the grey line at the right-hand edge.
See itKeep kBT/ε = 0.20 and w = 1000, and move p0 to 0.13. Watch for: Ē/ε reading 0.870, −TS/ε reading −1.279 and F/ε reading −0.409, with the circle at the bottom of the heavy curve.
07

The crossover sits at kBT = ε/ln w

The ground state and the excited level hold equal probability when their weights match, w e−ε/kBT = 1. That puts p0eq at ½, and solving for the temperature gives the crossover below. This follows from the model; the notes supply the weight w e−βE it rests on.

Where the level’s weight equals the ground state’s.

It is 0.434 ε for w = 10, 0.217 ε for w = 100 and 0.145 ε for w = 1000. Since ln 100 = 2 ln 10 and ln 1000 = 3 ln 10, the crossover falls to a half and a third of its w = 10 value, not to a tenth and a hundredth. In the sim’s sweep at w = 1000, p0eq reads 0.559 at 0.14 ε and 0.440 at 0.15 ε. For w = 1 there is no crossing in the range, since p0eq stays above 0.88 up to 0.50 ε.

p0eq against kBT/ε, as in the strip below the chart, for all four values of w.
See itSet w to 1000 and kBT/ε to 0.14, with p0 at 0.56. Watch for: p0eq reading 0.559, just above one half, and the dot on the strip sitting above the half-way height.
See itSet w to 1000 and kBT/ε to 0.15, with p0 at 0.44. Watch for: p0eq reading 0.440, just below one half, and the dot on the strip now below that height.
08

Where it matters

  • Excited levels with many states. A level with many states is occupied at a lower temperature than its gap alone suggests. For a gap of 0.100 eV, w = 1000 puts the crossover at 0.145 ε, about 168 K, while for w = 1 there is no crossover at any temperature: p0eq is still 0.731 at kBT = ε, near 1160 K.
  • Low and high temperature. As T falls, the sum Z is dominated by the lowest level and F tends to its energy; as T rises, the entropy term dominates and the gaps matter less (notes 4.5). At kBT/ε = 0.05 the sim has p0eq = 1.000 for every w.
  • Two forms of one substance. A form with lower energy and a form with more states have equal free energies at a temperature set by the gap and the ratio of their numbers of states.
Go deeper: why the crossover is exact

Rewrite F with the w-dependence collected into one factor:

F/ε for the trial, with t = kBT/ε.

The last bracket is symmetric under p0 ↔ 1 − p0. The factor 1 − (kBT/ε) ln w multiplies (1 − p0) alone: the energy cost of moving probability into the level, net of the entropy that w supplies. Setting dF/dp0 = 0 gives p0/(1 − p0) = eε/kBT/w, the Boltzmann value. At kBT = ε/ln w the factor vanishes, only the symmetric bracket is left, and the minimum falls at p0 = ½.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim plots the mean energy, the entropy term and the free energy of a trial distribution over a ground state and a w-fold excited level, against p0, at a temperature and w you choose.

Key points

  • F = Ē − TS is lowest at p0eq = 1/(1 + w e−ε/kBT), where F = −kBT ln Z.
  • The level counts w times, so its weight is w e−ε/kBT; at w = 1000 and 0.20 ε it holds 87% of the probability.
  • Ē rises as probability leaves the ground state, but −TS falls further; the two weights are equal at kBT = ε/ln w.

Common mix-ups

  • “Each excited state is unlikely, so the level stays empty.” At w = 1000 and 0.20 ε, p0eq = 0.129, so the level holds 87%.
  • “Spreading the probability lowers the energy.” Ē rises, by 0.870 ε; F falls because −TS falls by 1.279 ε.
  • “p0eq is 1/(1 + w).” That leaves out the Boltzmann factor. The denominator is 1 + 6.74, not 1001.

Things to try on your own

  • With w = 1 and kBT/ε = 0.20, drag the grey line along the chart and find where F is lowest.
  • At w = 100, sweep kBT/ε down from 0.50 and find where p0eq passes ½.
  • Predict p0eq for w = 10 at kBT/ε = 0.30 from Z, then set it and check the readout.
